q: A phlebotomist finishes a draw at the bedside. When should the tubes be labeled?
choices: After returning to the laboratory so the labels stay clean
Before the draw, so the tubes are ready to go
At the bedside, immediately after the draw and before leaving the patient
At the time the specimen is logged into the LIS
why: Labeling occurs at the point of collection in the presence of the patient, which is the only way to guarantee the tube matches the patient. Labeling before the draw is wrong because an unused or aborted tube could then be filled with another patient's blood.

q: A tube arrives in the laboratory with a legible label but the patient name does not match the name on the requisition. What is the correct action?
choices: Reject the specimen, notify the ordering unit, and document the discrepancy
Correct the tube label to match the requisition and process it
Process the specimen and add a comment to the report
Ask the nurse to verbally confirm which name is right, then relabel
why: A mislabeled specimen cannot be corrected by anyone other than the original collector at the bedside, so it is rejected, documented, and the unit is notified for recollection. Relabeling from the requisition is prohibited because it only guesses at identity and can transfer a fatal error into the result.

q: A red-top serum tube is drawn at 0800. How long should it sit before centrifugation?
choices: Spin immediately to save turnaround time
5 to 10 minutes
15 minutes maximum
30 to 60 minutes at room temperature to allow complete clotting
why: Serum tubes need 30 to 60 minutes at room temperature for the clot to fully form before spinning. Spinning early leaves fibrin that continues to clot in the serum, producing latent fibrin strands that clog analyzer probes.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes serum from plasma?
choices: Serum contains fibrinogen; plasma does not
Serum is from a clotted, non-anticoagulated tube and lacks fibrinogen; plasma is from an anticoagulated tube and contains fibrinogen
Plasma comes from a red-top tube and serum from a lavender-top tube
Serum and plasma are chemically identical, only the tube color differs
why: Clotting consumes fibrinogen, so serum has none, while an anticoagulated tube prevents clotting and leaves fibrinogen in the plasma. The first choice reverses the relationship, which is a classic trap.

q: A phlebotomist has only one tube to centrifuge. What must be done before starting the spin?
choices: Place a balance tube of equal size filled with water to the same level opposite it
Spin the single tube at half speed
Place the tube in the center well of the rotor
Run the centrifuge with the lid open to monitor it
why: The rotor must be balanced by weight and position, so a water-filled tube of the same size and fill level goes directly opposite. Reducing the speed does not correct an unbalanced load and can still damage the rotor and break tubes.

q: A typical laboratory centrifuge setting for separating a serum gel tube is about:
choices: 1000 rpm for 2 minutes
1500 rpm for 20 minutes
3000 rpm for 10 minutes, following the manufacturer's instructions
5000 rpm for 15 minutes
why: About 3000 rpm for 10 minutes is the common specification, but the tube and centrifuge manufacturer's directions always govern. Lower speed or shorter time gives incomplete separation and a poor gel barrier.

q: A gel separator tube was spun once, and the barrier looks incomplete. The technician wants to spin it again. What is correct?
choices: Re-spin at a higher speed to force the gel down
Do not re-spin a gel tube; recollect the specimen if separation is inadequate
Re-spin for double the original time
Invert the tube and re-spin it upside down
why: Re-spinning a gel tube can force analytes, especially potassium, out of cells trapped above or within the gel and falsely alter results. Higher speed does not fix the barrier and simply compounds the contamination.

q: The centrifuge timer ends but the rotor is still coasting. What should the phlebotomist do?
choices: Open the lid and brake the rotor by hand to save time
Open the lid as soon as the timer stops
Open the lid and remove only the outer tubes
Wait until the rotor comes to a complete stop on its own before opening the lid
why: Opening the lid or stopping the rotor by hand creates aerosols and can cause injury and tube breakage. Waiting for a full stop is the only safe practice, regardless of turnaround pressure.

q: A serum specimen is drawn at 0900 and remains unspun on the counter. By what time must the serum be separated from the cells?
choices: 1100, which is 2 hours from the time of collection
There is no limit as long as the tube is capped
why: The standard is separation of serum or plasma from cells within 2 hours of collection. Leaving cells in contact longer allows glycolysis and cellular leakage that invalidate several chemistry results.

q: A potassium and glucose specimen sat with cells in contact for 4 hours. What results are expected?
choices: Both potassium and glucose falsely elevated
Potassium falsely elevated and glucose falsely decreased by roughly 10 mg/dL per hour
Potassium falsely decreased and glucose falsely increased
Neither analyte is affected if the tube stayed capped
why: Red cells leak potassium into the serum while continuing glycolysis, consuming glucose at roughly 10 mg/dL per hour. Assuming a capped tube protects the sample is wrong because the change is cellular metabolism, not evaporation.

q: Which group of tests requires the specimen to be chilled in an ice slurry during transport?
choices: Potassium, calcium, and magnesium
Bilirubin, folate, and vitamin B12
Ammonia, lactic acid, arterial blood gas, PTH, and gastrin
Cold agglutinins and cryoglobulins
why: Ammonia, lactic acid, ABG, PTH, and gastrin are all unstable at room temperature and are chilled to slow metabolism and degradation. Cold agglutinins and cryoglobulins are the opposite case and must be kept at body temperature.

q: A phlebotomist places a lavender-top chemistry specimen for potassium on ice. Why is this incorrect?
choices: Chilling causes red cells to release potassium, falsely elevating the result
Chilling causes potassium to bind to the tube wall, falsely lowering the result
Chilling has no measurable effect on potassium
Chilling causes the EDTA to precipitate
why: Cold inhibits the cell membrane sodium-potassium pump, so potassium leaks out of the cells and the measured value rises falsely. It is not a falsely low value, which is the distractor most students pick by analogy to glucose.

q: Which specimens must be protected from light during transport and storage?
choices: Ammonia and lactic acid
Cold agglutinins and cryoglobulins
PT and PTT specimens
Bilirubin, vitamin B12, folate, and carotene
why: Bilirubin, vitamin B12, folate, and carotene photodegrade, so they are wrapped in foil or placed in an amber container. Ammonia and lactic acid need chilling rather than light protection.

q: A cryoglobulin specimen is collected. How must it be handled before processing?
choices: Placed in an ice slurry immediately
Refrigerated at 2 to 8 C
Kept at 37 C body temperature until the serum is separated
Frozen at -20 C within 30 minutes
why: Cryoglobulins and cold agglutinins precipitate or attach to cells when cooled, so the specimen stays at 37 C using a warming block or pre-warmed tube until separation. Icing would remove the very protein the test is designed to detect.

q: A phlebotomist pours serum from a spun gel tube into a labeled transfer tube for a send-out test. What must the aliquot label contain?
choices: Only the accession number, since the parent tube has the rest
The same patient identifiers and accession information as the original tube
The technician's initials only
A new accession number generated at the time of pouring
why: Every aliquot carries the full identification of the parent specimen so identity is never lost at any step. An accession number alone is insufficient if the tube leaves the facility or the label is questioned.

q: Two tubes of serum from the same patient are short-draw. May they be combined into one aliquot tube to make enough volume?
choices: No. Pooling specimens is not permitted, even from the same patient, because collection times and additives may differ
Yes, as long as both tubes are the same color
Yes, if the technician documents the pooling
Yes, if both tubes were drawn within 2 hours of each other
why: Pooling destroys the one-to-one link between a result and a single documented collection event and can mix different draw times or additives. Same tube color does not make the two collections interchangeable.

q: A CBC in a lavender-top tube is collected on the floor. What is the usual acceptable limit for testing a room-temperature EDTA specimen?
choices: 30 minutes
2 hours only
8 hours only
Within 24 hours, though within a few hours is preferred for accurate cell morphology
why: Routine CBC counts remain acceptable up to about 24 hours at room temperature, but morphology on the smear deteriorates well before then, so prompt testing is preferred. Claiming a hard 30-minute limit confuses CBC with the tighter coagulation rules.

q: A light-blue-top tube is collected for a PTT and is not centrifuged. What is the maximum time to testing?
choices: 1 hour
2 hours
4 hours
24 hours
why: An unspun PTT must be tested within 4 hours because heparin and labile factors degrade quickly. The 24-hour window belongs to the PT, which is the far more stable of the two.

q: Which specimen should NOT be sent through a pneumatic tube system?
choices: A routine CBC in a lavender tube
A specimen for cold agglutinins or one that is hemolysis-sensitive, and any glass or leaking container
A spun chemistry gel tube
A urinalysis in a sealed container
why: Pneumatic tube acceleration and impact cause hemolysis and can break glass or force a leaking container open, and temperature-critical specimens cannot be maintained in transit. Routine spun chemistry and CBC tubes are generally acceptable in a validated system.

q: How should a requisition be transported with its specimen in a biohazard transport bag?
choices: Folded around the tube inside the main compartment
Taped to the outside of the tube
Placed loose in the same compartment as the specimen
In the separate outside pouch of the bag, away from the specimen compartment
why: The paperwork goes in the outer pouch so a leak cannot contaminate or destroy the documentation. Placing it in with the tube risks illegible, biohazardous paperwork if the specimen leaks.

q: A diagnostic blood specimen is being shipped to a reference laboratory by courier. Which classification and packaging applies?
choices: Category B, UN3373, using triple packaging with a leakproof primary receptacle, absorbent material, a leakproof secondary container, and a rigid outer box
Category A, UN2814, single container
No classification is required for patient specimens
Category B, UN1845, double packaging
why: Routine diagnostic specimens are Category B, marked UN3373, and require the triple packaging system. UN2814 is Category A, reserved for substances capable of causing permanent disability or life-threatening disease, and UN1845 is the number for dry ice, not a specimen class.

q: Frozen specimens are being shipped on dry ice. Which statement is correct?
choices: Dry ice should be sealed airtight to prevent sublimation
Dry ice is placed inside the secondary container with the specimen
Dry ice goes outside the secondary container, and the package must allow carbon dioxide gas to vent
Dry ice may be used only for room-temperature specimens
why: Dry ice is a refrigerant placed outside the secondary container, and the outer package must vent sublimating carbon dioxide or it can rupture. An airtight seal is specifically prohibited for this reason.

q: A specimen is to be stored refrigerated. What temperature range applies?
choices: 15 to 30 C
2 to 8 C
-20 C or below
0 to 1 C
why: Refrigerated storage is 2 to 8 C, room temperature is 15 to 30 C, and frozen is -20 C or below. Choosing 15 to 30 C describes ambient storage, not refrigeration.

q: A frozen aliquot has been thawed and refrozen twice while waiting for a send-out run. Why is this a problem?
choices: Repeated freeze-thaw cycles denature proteins and degrade analytes, invalidating results
Repeated freezing concentrates the specimen and raises all values equally
Freeze-thaw cycles only affect the label adhesive
There is no effect as long as the specimen stays below -20 C between thaws
why: Each freeze-thaw cycle damages protein structure and destroys labile analytes, so specimens are aliquoted into single-use portions before freezing. The idea that values simply rise uniformly is false, since the effect is analyte-specific degradation.

q: A light-blue-top coagulation tube arrives with a visible clot. What is the appropriate action?
choices: Break up the clot with an applicator stick and test it
Spin it longer and test the plasma above the clot
Test it and note the clot on the report
Reject the specimen, document the reason, and request recollection
why: A clotted anticoagulated tube has already consumed the clotting factors being measured, so the result is meaningless and the specimen is rejected and documented. Dislodging the clot does not restore the consumed factors and adds hemolysis.

q: Which of the following is NOT a standard specimen rejection criterion?
choices: Grossly hemolyzed serum for a potassium test
A tube filled to its full stated draw volume
Quantity not sufficient for the ordered test
Blood collected in an expired tube
why: A properly filled tube is exactly what is wanted; rejection applies to hemolysis, QNS, expired tubes, clots, wrong tube type, and identification problems. A full tube is only an issue in coagulation if the ratio is off, which is a short-draw problem, not a full-draw one.

q: After rejecting a specimen, what documentation is required?
choices: Nothing, since the specimen was never tested
A verbal note to the next shift
The reason for rejection, the date and time, the person notified, and the notification time, recorded in the LIS or rejection log
Only the accession number crossed off the log
why: Rejection is a reportable preanalytical event that must be documented with reason, time, and who was notified so recollection happens and trends can be tracked. Verbal notification alone leaves no record and no accountability.

q: A blood alcohol specimen is collected for a legal case. What does chain of custody require?
choices: A documented, unbroken record of every person who handled the specimen, with dates, times, and signatures, in a sealed and initialed container
Only that the specimen be labeled and refrigerated
That the specimen be tested in duplicate
That a supervisor draw the specimen
why: Chain of custody is a legal document tracking possession from collection through testing and storage with signatures at each transfer, and the tamper-evident seal is initialed by the collector. Labeling and refrigeration are ordinary handling and do not establish legal custody.

q: A STAT troponin arrives in the laboratory. How should it be handled?
choices: Placed in the routine rack and worked in order of arrival
Given priority handling, logged and processed immediately, with turnaround time tracked from receipt
Held until a batch of chemistry specimens accumulates
Sent to the reference laboratory for faster analysis
why: STAT specimens bypass the routine queue and are processed immediately because the result drives urgent clinical decisions, and turnaround time is a monitored quality indicator. Batching defeats the entire purpose of a STAT order.

q: A patient's hemoglobin today is 14.2 g/dL, but yesterday's value was 8.1 g/dL with no transfusion documented. What quality process flags this?
choices: Levey-Jennings chart
Proficiency testing
Calibration verification
A delta check, which compares a current result to the same patient's previous result
why: A delta check compares consecutive results on the same patient and flags implausible shifts that often signal a mislabeled or switched specimen. Levey-Jennings charts monitor control material over time, not an individual patient's consecutive values.

q: Collecting the specimen, labeling it, and transporting it to the laboratory belong to which phase of testing?
choices: Analytical
Postanalytical
Preanalytical
Interpretive
why: Everything before the instrument runs the sample is preanalytical, and it accounts for the majority of laboratory errors. The analytical phase is the actual measurement, and reporting the result is postanalytical.

q: A critical potassium value of 7.2 mmol/L is called to the nursing unit. What must occur to complete the notification?
choices: The receiver repeats the patient name, test, and value back, and the caller documents the read-back, the time, and the receiver's name
The caller leaves a voicemail and documents the call time
The value is faxed and the fax confirmation is filed
The value is flagged in the LIS for the physician to see at the next login
why: Critical values require direct communication with read-back verification by the receiver, documented with time and name. A voicemail or a passive LIS flag does not confirm that a responsible person actually received and understood the value.

q: A transport bag is opened and the tube inside is cracked and leaking. What is the first action?
choices: Pour the remaining blood into a clean tube and relabel it
Keep the bag closed, don gloves and appropriate PPE, and handle it inside a biological safety cabinet or contained area per policy, then discard and request recollection
Wipe the tube with a paper towel and run the test
Place the bag in the refrigerator until a supervisor arrives
why: A leaking specimen is an exposure hazard, so it is contained with PPE, discarded, and recollected while the incident is documented. Transferring leaked blood to a new tube both risks exposure and produces a specimen of uncertain identity and integrity.

q: A tube broke inside the centrifuge. After the rotor stops and PPE is donned, how is the centrifuge decontaminated?
choices: Rinse the chamber with hot water only
Wipe with alcohol and resume use immediately
Remove glass with forceps or a brush, then disinfect the chamber, cups, and rotor with a 1:10 bleach solution or approved tuberculocidal disinfectant and allow the contact time
Spray with a deodorizer and close the lid
why: Broken glass is never picked up by hand, and the chamber requires an approved disinfectant left for the labeled contact time to be effective. Alcohol wiping alone does not meet the contact time or the tuberculocidal requirement for blood spills.

q: A specimen is received in the laboratory. What does accessioning accomplish?
choices: It establishes the reference range for the test
It replaces the need for a requisition
It substitutes for patient identification at the bedside
It assigns a unique identifying number that links the specimen, the patient, the requisition, and the test order in the LIS, with a documented receipt time
why: Accessioning creates the unique number that ties specimen, patient, and order together and time-stamps receipt for turnaround tracking. It does not replace the requisition or the bedside identification that already established whose blood is in the tube.
